clue.text: It's no magic carpet it controls in flight

definitions.text: It's no magic carpet it controls in flight

parts.words: It's no magic carpet it controls in flight
parts.note: the flight is a staircase, not air travel: the thing in question holds a stair carpet in place at the back of each tread

explanation.surface: A riddle about something that steers a flying carpet through the air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight' suggests flying, so 'magic carpet' seems in scene; but a flight is a run of stairs, and a stair rod is the metal bar that keeps the carpet in the angle of each step.
explanation.definitionFit: A brass bar laid across a step keeps the runner of a staircase carpet fixed, so it controls carpet on a flight.

clue.text: Bulb holder soundly encourages giving it a bash

indicators.note: soundly signals that the urging words are said out loud to give the fitting

parts.note: sock it! urges someone to hit something hard

explanation.surface: Someone urges a friend to smash a light bulb's holder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soundly' looks like 'thoroughly' but signals a homophone: 'sock it' (hit it) said out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: A light bulb is screwed or pushed into a fitting that holds it and supplies power.

clue.text: Might Granny Smith be upset with this play?

definitions.text: Might Granny Smith be upset with this play

parts.words: Might Granny Smith be upset with this play
parts.note: Granny Smith is a variety of fruit that could be upset from a barrow, and 'upset the barrow' is an idiom; Shaw wrote a political comedy of the same name

explanation.surface: Would an elderly woman named Smith be offended by a theatre production?
explanation.walkthrough: Granny Smith seems a person who might be offended; it is an apple variety, which could be upset from a fruit barrow. The Apple Cart is a 1928 play by George Bernard Shaw.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's comedy has this title, and a Granny Smith is a fruit that would be carried on such a barrow.

clue.text: Manners graceful here

parts.note: Manners is the family name of the Dukes who take their title from this small English county, and dukes are addressed as Your Grace

explanation.surface: A place where people's manners are elegant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manners' looks like etiquette but is the surname of the Dukes of Rutland; 'graceful' means having a Grace, i.e. a duke. Rutland is England's smallest county.
explanation.definitionFit: The Manners family hold the dukedom named after this smallest English county, so its Graces belong here.

clue.text: Looked fondly at Sir Oliver, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the surname might be put another way, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: Sir Oliver Lodge was a British physicist and radio pioneer

explanation.surface: Someone gazed admiringly at a knight called Sir Oliver.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Oliver Lodge was a physicist; 'perhaps' asks for his surname LODGE rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To ogle is to eye someone amorously or with obvious desire, gazing fondly.

clue.text: Stuck like a picnic sandwich ?

explanation.surface: Something wedged fast, compared to a sandwich packed for a picnic.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuck fast means wedged or blocked; a sandwich spread with fruit preserve is filled that way.

clue.text: Each family-proud Scot traces his course

definitions.text: Each family-proud Scot traces his course

parts.words: Each family-proud Scot traces his course
parts.note: a Scot proud of his family traces his own lineage, Scots ain meaning own; spoken with each as a, the phrase gives the name of a famous racecourse

explanation.surface: Every Scot proud of his family follows its line of descent.
explanation.walkthrough: The held clue had 'London WC 2 A' spliced in from the page; the scan shows it without. A proud Scot traces his 'ain tree' (own family tree); the word is the Merseyside racecourse of the Grand National.
explanation.definitionFit: The Merseyside racing venue hosts the Grand National steeplechase, a famous horse-racing course.

clue.text: The safest milk is in the cow-that's the maxim

indicators.note: is in means the milk is placed inside the cow's call

parts.note: a cow says moo
TT stands for tuberculin-tested, a guarantee of safe milk

explanation.surface: A dairy saying that milk is safest while still inside the animal.
explanation.walkthrough: TT, for tuberculin-tested, was the label on British milk certified free of tuberculosis; 'is in' sets it inside the cow's call.
explanation.definitionFit: A short saying expressing a rule of conduct is a maxim or watchword.

clue.text: Glory be …

parts.note: the words open a short hymn of praise to the Trinity sung at the end of psalms

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise, trailing off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glory be!' reads as an exclamation; it is the start of the Gloria Patri, the standard short hymn of praise in Christian liturgy.
explanation.definitionFit: A liturgical formula of praise to God, such as the Gloria Patri, is a hymn of glorification.

clue.text: Morning help reorganized in small part by a treatise

indicators.note: in means the morning and reworked help go inside the short form of part

parts.note: pt is the abbreviation, a small form, of part

indicators.note: reorganized means the letters of help are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Domestic morning help, reorganised, partly responsible for a treatise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reorganized' turns HELP into PHLE; AM + PHLE go 'in' PT, the abbreviated ('small') part. 'by a' joins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A short printed booklet arguing a case is a brief treatise or tract.

clue.text: Invented by a "Heads I win " Chancellor ?

definitions.text: Invented by a "Heads I win " Chancellor ?

parts.words: Invented by a "Heads I win " Chancellor ?
parts.note: heads are capitals and 'I win' is gains: a finance minister who wins whichever way the coin falls would devise a levy on profits from selling assets

explanation.surface: A coin-tossing finance minister who rigs the game so that he always comes out ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads I win (tails you lose)' is the rigged bet; read literally, heads are capitals and winning is gaining, and the Chancellor of the Exchequer is the UK finance minister who sets taxes.
explanation.definitionFit: A levy on the profit from selling assets is the sort of duty a finance minister introduces, and its words echo capitals and winnings.

clue.text: A mere lad, uncommonly green and precious

indicators.note: uncommonly means in an unusual way, so the letters of the three words are set out unusually

explanation.surface: A mere boy who is unusually naive yet valuable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncommonly' rearranges the letters of A MERE LAD; 'green' looks like naivety in the surface but is the colour of the gem.
explanation.definitionFit: The gemstone is a precious stone of bright green colour.

clue.text: Coddle Rob perhaps in Simon's fishing vessel

indicators.note: in means the reworked letters are placed within the vessel

parts.note: in the nursery rhyme Simple Simon went fishing for a whale, but all the water he had got was in his mother's pail

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the name might be spelt otherwise, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Pampering a man called Rob aboard Simon's fishing boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges the name, and 'in' puts it inside the vessel, which is the pail from the nursery rhyme 'Simple Simon', not a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: To coddle an egg is to cook it gently in water just below boiling, much as partly cooking food does.

clue.text: France's rich place had one such point

definitions.text: France's rich place had one such point

parts.words: France's rich place had one such point
parts.note: rich plus place, in French lieu, gives Richelieu, the churchman who ran France under Louis XIII; a compass point of the same rank is north, south, east or west

explanation.surface: A wealthy French estate that had a certain kind of feature.
explanation.walkthrough: Rich + lieu (French for 'place') is Richelieu, a cardinal; the four main compass points are the cardinal points, so the word serves both readings.
explanation.definitionFit: Richelieu held the rank of a senior Roman Catholic prelate, and north, south, east and west are the principal compass points.

clue.text: Brandy at 20 francs ?

explanation.surface: Paying twenty francs for a glass of cognac.
explanation.definitionFit: A grade of cognac bears the emperor's name, and a French gold coin worth twenty francs was named after him.

clue.text: Supplementing this out of relations inside for example

indicators.note: inside means the relations are placed within the abbreviation for example

parts.note: e.g. is the abbreviation for exempli gratia, for example
kin means relations, one's family

explanation.surface: Supplementing family income from relations, as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this out' stands for the answer followed by 'out': to eke out is to supplement. KIN goes 'inside' EG.
explanation.definitionFit: To eke out a supply is to make it stretch further by adding to it, so the phrase means supplementing.

clue.text: In a trance maybe, but far from disembodied

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters could be arranged otherwise, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A medium in a trance, yet physically present rather than a ghost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges IN A TRANCE; the trance suggests a spirit medium, yet the answer means in the flesh.
explanation.definitionFit: Incarnate means embodied in flesh, the opposite of a spirit without a body.

clue.text: Recall one of the Sappers' Society

parts.note: the Sappers are the Royal Engineers, RE
one of the society is a member of it

explanation.surface: Thinking back to a fellow of the Royal Engineers' club.
explanation.walkthrough: Sappers is the nickname of the Royal Engineers, RE; one of the Society is a MEMBER, with 'Society' completing that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To recall something is to bring it back to mind.

clue.text: Praise the erstwhile endless road tax

parts.note: ex means former or erstwhile, as in an ex-husband

indicators.note: endless means the last letter of the charge is cut off

parts.note: a toll is a charge for using a road

explanation.surface: Singing the praises of a road tax that has now been abolished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' trims the final letter from the road charge; 'the erstwhile' is a former thing, an ex.
explanation.definitionFit: To praise someone highly is to laud or glorify them.

clue.text: German siren

parts.note: the legendary maiden on a Rhine rock whose song lured boatmen to their deaths

explanation.surface: A warning siren made in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'siren' could be an alarm; here it is the enchantress of German legend who sang from a rock on the Rhine.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhine maiden of legend lured sailors to shipwreck with her singing, as the sirens of Greek myth did.

clue.text: Poor pay for the young P.M. with ancestral origins

parts.note: William Pitt the Younger was British Prime Minister at 24

indicators.note: the origins of the word ancestral are its opening letters, so only its start is taken

explanation.surface: A meagre salary for a youthful Prime Minister with a distinguished pedigree.
explanation.walkthrough: Pitt the Younger was the youngest British Prime Minister; 'origins' takes ANCE, the opening four letters of 'ancestral'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny, inadequate wage or allowance is a poor sum of money.

clue.text: Harass a hundred, if flat out

indicators.note: out means the letters are put out of order

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: Pestering a hundred people if they are flatly refused.
explanation.walkthrough: C (Roman 100) joins IF FLAT, and 'out' mixes all seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To afflict is to trouble or torment someone, to harass them.

clue.text: He did wrong to return

indicators.note: to return means the word for having done wrong is read backwards

parts.note: to sin is to do wrong

explanation.surface: A man who did wrong comes back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' stands for any man's name; 'to return' reads SINNED backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A male first name stands for a man, so 'He' is defined by an example name.

clue.text: Charm into bondage

explanation.surface: Captivating someone so much that it amounts to slavery.
explanation.definitionFit: To captivate is to charm; the word literally means putting into thrall, the old term for slavery.

clue.text: Roman, if non-U, birds

indicators.note: if non-U says that without the letter U the answer would be the birds, so U is put into them

parts.note: tits are small songbirds

explanation.surface: A Roman who is not upper-class, among birds.
explanation.walkthrough: Non-U is British slang for not upper-class; here it says the answer with no U is TITS. Titus was a Roman emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: Titus was a first-century emperor of Rome, a Roman by name.

clue.text: Whistler's a sportsman

parts.note: the whistler is not the American painter but an official on the field who blows a whistle to control play

explanation.surface: A claim that the painter Whistler was a keen sportsman.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital W makes 'Whistler' look like James McNeill Whistler, the painter; the person who blows the whistle in a match is the umpiring official.
explanation.definitionFit: The official in charge of a football or rugby match blows a whistle and takes part in the sport.

clue.text: Gunners are in, in Morocco

definitions.note: the definition names a place found in Morocco

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, the Gunners
in cricket the side that is in bats

explanation.surface: Artillerymen have arrived in Morocco.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the side that is 'in' is batting; Rabat is the capital of Morocco.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabat is the capital city of Morocco.

clue.text: Wherein few were winners

parts.note: echoes Churchill's 1940 tribute to the RAF pilots: never was so much owed by so many to so few

explanation.surface: A contest in which only a handful of competitors won.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The few' is Churchill's name for the RAF fighter pilots who won the 1940 air campaign over southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1940 air campaign over England was won by a small band of fighter pilots, Churchill's 'few'.

clue.text: Hodge develops citrus

indicators.note: develops means the letters of citrus grow into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A man named Hodge cultivates citrus fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: Hodge is the traditional name for a typical English farm labourer; 'develops' rearranges CITRUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Hodge is the stock name for a country farmhand, a simple countryman.

clue.text: Before those making disapproving noises Bob is a bit tongue-tied

indicators.note: before means the shilling goes in front of the people tutting

parts.note: a bob is old British slang for a shilling, abbreviated s
tutters are people who say tut-tut in disapproval

explanation.surface: Bob is a little lost for words in front of a disapproving crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a name but is slang for a shilling, the old British coin written s; 'Before' puts it ahead of TUTTERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who repeats sounds and halts when speaking is partly unable to get words out.
